prompt: A mid-size regional hospital system posts a role titled "Digital Accessibility Analyst" for the first time in its history. Which of these is the most likely actual driver, and why does it matter for how you'd pitch yourself?

options.text: A senior developer personally became passionate about inclusive design
The organisation is a public accommodation covered by ADA Title III, or receives federal funds and is covered by Section 504/508, and legal or compliance flagged exposure on the patient portal
Screen reader users complained loudly enough on social media to force a hire
The role is decorative — hospitals rarely act on accessibility hires

hints: Ask who signs off on a first-ever role like this — usually not engineering alone.
Healthcare orgs sit under more overlapping accessibility obligations than almost any other sector: patient portals, federal funding strings, and public-accommodation status.
explanation: Legal or compliance exposure is the most common real trigger for a *first* accessibility hire, especially in healthcare, higher-ed and government-adjacent organisations — sectors with an unusually dense stack of obligations (ADA Title III as a public accommodation, Section 504/508 if federal funds are involved, and increasingly state-level digital accessibility law). That doesn't make the hire cynical or the work meaningless; it means your first conversation with legal or compliance matters as much as your first conversation with engineering, and your pitch should speak fluently to both. A developer's personal interest can start a project, but it rarely creates a funded headcount on its own — funded headcount usually means someone above engineering decided the risk of not hiring was higher than the cost of hiring.

prompt: True or false: an in-house accessibility role is always the most stable option, because it comes with a fixed salary and a single employer.

config.statement: In-house is always the most stable accessibility career route.
config.rubric: A full answer states the verdict and names at least one concrete way stability can fail in-house, and one way it can hold up outside it.

hints: "Stable" has more than one axis: income, workload, and whether the role survives the next reorg.
A single-employer role concentrates risk in one place. A freelance practice with three retainer clients doesn't.
explanation: False, and the useful version says why. In-house pays predictably month to month, but accessibility teams are frequently the first cut in a reorg — the role is a cost centre until someone re-explains why it isn't, and that argument has to be made again every budget cycle. A freelance practice with several retainer clients loses income unevenly if one client leaves, not all at once, which is a different and often gentler kind of risk. Neither route is inherently more stable; they are stable against different things. In-house is stable against income variance month to month and unstable against a single bad reorg. Freelance is the reverse.

prompt: Match each adjacent role to the accessibility QA skill it draws on most directly.

pairs.right: Running and interpreting sessions with disabled users, distinguishing a barrier from a preference
Knowing which barriers a scanner can and can't reliably catch
Reading a VPAT or Accessibility Conformance Report against what you'd actually find in an audit
Translating findings into something a product owner can rank and act on

hints: Each adjacent role takes one slice of the full audit skill and goes deep on it, rather than needing all of it.
The procurement role is closest to reading, not producing, findings — it's the same judgement in reverse.
explanation: None of these are a different skill from the ground up — they're the same underlying judgement (what actually blocks a task, and how confident can you be about it) applied in a narrower lane. That's why this skill opens more doors than the job title "accessibility auditor" suggests: a QA automation engineer who understands the automated/manual boundary writes far better test suites than one who doesn't, and a procurement reviewer who has actually run an audit can tell a real VPAT from a template filled in by someone who never tested anything.

prompt: A prospective client asks you to quote a flat fee for "a full accessibility audit" of their site with no further detail. Write the two or three questions you'd ask before naming a number, and explain what a number given without those answers actually risks.
hints: What varies the cost of an audit more than almost anything else? Scope.
"The whole site" is not a scope — how many distinct page templates and user journeys does that actually mean?
Which methods are included changes the price a lot: automated-only, automated plus manual, manual plus screen reader and keyboard testing all cost different amounts of your time.
explanation:
A defensible set of questions: how many distinct page templates or journeys does "the site" actually cover (not raw page count — a site with 400 near-identical product pages is one template, not 400 findings); which methods are in scope (automated scan, manual review, keyboard and screen reader testing, or all of them); and what happens after delivery — is a retest included, or is this a one-time snapshot?

A flat number given without those answers risks two things, both bad in different directions: you under-quote and end up doing a full manual-plus-assistive-technology audit for the price of an automated scan, or you over-quote defensively and lose the client to someone who asked better questions and priced accurately. Neither serves you as well as pricing against a scoped set of journeys and named methods, which is also the number you can defend if the client pushes back later.

prompt: Put these signals of a job posting's remote/async claim in order from weakest evidence to strongest.

items: The word "remote" appears once in the listing
The listing says "remote-first" and lists a specific timezone overlap window instead of "must be available 9-5 ET"
The interview process itself includes an async or take-home stage rather than only live calls
Current employees in the role you're applying for post publicly about working async, with specifics (which tools, how meetings are handled)

hints: A single word in a job ad costs the company nothing to write. What costs them something to build?
The interview process is a preview of the actual working culture — a company that can't run an async interview usually can't run an async team.
explanation: The weakest evidence is free to produce: the word "remote" appears on almost every listing now, including ones that mean "remote, but every meeting is live and mandatory." A named overlap window is more specific and slightly costlier to fake. The interview process is a genuine preview — a company whose entire interview loop is synchronous calls is very likely to run day-to-day work the same way, whatever the posting says. Public, specific testimony from someone actually doing the job is the strongest signal available before you're inside, because it's the hardest of the four to fabricate convincingly.

prompt: Sort each career situation into the route it fits best right now.

items.text: Wants full health benefits and a predictable schedule above almost everything else
Wants variety across many clients and industries, and doesn't mind travel or billable-hour tracking
Needs to build their schedule around unpredictable flare days and can't commit to fixed hours
Is new to the field and wants structured mentorship from senior reviewers
Already has two retainer clients and wants to add a third without giving up control of their calendar
Wants to influence a single product's roadmap over years, not just audit it once

hints: A route fits a person, not the field. Read for what each situation actually needs, not which route sounds most "real."
explanation: There's no universally better route — only a better fit for what a specific situation needs. Benefits and predictability point in-house; structured mentorship and variety point agency; control over one's own hours points freelance. The mistake worth naming: treating freelance as the fallback for people who "couldn't get a real job" is common and wrong — for someone managing variable capacity, freelance is often the only route where the schedule bends around the person instead of the reverse.

prompt: Someone with two years of manual QA experience and no accessibility-specific title wants to move into this field. Which adjacent-role pivot is most realistic as a first step?

options.text: Apply directly for Head of Accessibility roles — the QA background transfers entirely
Move into an accessibility-focused QA or test automation role, where the existing QA skill is the majority of the job
Wait until they hold an IAAP certification before applying to anything
Pivot to UX research, since QA and research use identical skills

hints: Which adjacent role keeps the most of what this person already knows how to do, and adds the least new skill on top?
explanation: Accessibility-focused QA or test automation keeps almost everything from a manual QA background — reading specs, writing reproducible bug reports, running structured test passes — and adds one focused new skill: knowing what to test for and why. That's a realistic next role, not a stretch. Head of Accessibility assumes years of domain leadership this person doesn't have yet. Certification can help later but isn't a prerequisite to a first role, and treating it as one wastes time that could be spent building a portfolio instead. UX research shares some skills with QA but is not identical — it centres interviewing and synthesis, which QA doesn't typically involve.

prompt: True or false: quoting an hourly rate is always more transparent, and therefore better for the client, than quoting a flat project fee.

config.statement: Hourly rates are always more transparent and better for the client than flat fees.
config.rubric: States the verdict and names a concrete downside of hourly pricing for the client.

hints: Who bears the risk if the work takes longer than expected — the client or the reviewer — under each pricing model?
Predictability of total cost is also a form of transparency.
explanation: False. Hourly billing is transparent about your time, but it shifts all the schedule risk onto the client: if the audit takes longer than estimated, their bill grows and they have no cap to plan against. A flat fee scoped to named journeys and methods gives the client a number they can budget against, and puts the estimating risk on the reviewer — which is exactly why scoping precisely, as covered earlier in this module, matters so much before naming that number. Neither model is unconditionally better; hourly suits open-ended or advisory work, flat fees suit a defined audit.

prompt: A listing says "competitive salary, fast-paced environment, must be a self-starter comfortable with ambiguity." Read against this module, what does this combination of phrases most likely signal?

options.text: A well-resourced, mature accessibility function with clear process
An unscoped role without a defined salary band or established process, where you'd be building the function from nothing
A remote-first, async-friendly culture
A role that specifically values disabled candidates' lived experience

hints: "Competitive salary" without a number is usually a sign the band isn't fixed, not that it's generous.
"Fast-paced" and "comfortable with ambiguity" are frequently doing the work of "we don't have a process for this yet."
explanation: This exact cluster of phrases is common in postings for a first accessibility hire at an organisation that hasn't built the function yet — which isn't automatically bad, but it's a very different job than joining an established team with a documented process, and it's worth knowing which one you're walking into before you accept. None of the phrases here say anything about pay transparency, remote culture, or disability inclusion specifically — reading them as positive signals on those axes is exactly the kind of posting-language optimism this lesson exists to correct.

prompt: You're deciding between two real openings: one in-house role at a healthcare company with a fixed \$85k salary and standard benefits, and one freelance retainer at roughly \$70/hr for an estimated 15 hours/week with no benefits. Name the two or three factors — beyond the raw numbers — that should actually decide this for someone managing a variable-energy chronic condition.
hints: Raw hourly-equivalent math ignores what happens on a bad week for each option.
One of these options has a hard floor if you can't work; the other doesn't.
Benefits aren't just money — for someone with an ongoing condition, health insurance terms can outweigh a salary gap entirely.
explanation: The raw math (roughly \$54,600/year for the freelance retainer at full hours vs \$85k salaried) undersells how differently the two options behave on a bad week. The salaried role pays the same whether this week is a good one or not — sick leave, once earned, doesn't require renegotiation. The freelance retainer's income is tied to hours actually worked, so a bad flare week is a pay cut, not just a hard week. Against that: the freelance retainer usually gives more control over exactly when those 15 hours happen, which the salaried role may not, especially early in a new role before trust is established. Health insurance terms matter enormously here too — a chronic condition can make employer-sponsored coverage worth more than the salary gap between the two options, in a way a simple hourly comparison completely misses. There's no universally correct answer; the actual decision hinges on which kind of risk (income variance vs schedule rigidity) a specific person's condition makes harder to absorb.

prompt: Put these steps of researching a target employer in the order that produces the most useful market document, cheapest first.

items: Check whether the organisation is covered by a specific accessibility obligation (public accommodation, federal funding, EU market access) that would explain why they'd hire for this
Read three of their live job postings for the exact language used about remote work, ambiguity and process
Search for current or former employees in accessibility roles there posting publicly about the work
Reach out directly to ask a specific, answerable question, rather than a general "are you hiring"

hints: The cheapest research is public and requires no reply from anyone — start there.
Direct outreach is the most expensive step in attention and social risk, so it belongs last, once you know enough to ask something specific.
explanation: This order moves from free public research to costlier, higher-signal steps. Checking the obligation takes minutes and tells you *why* a role might exist at all. Reading postings costs a little more time and reveals the culture-language patterns from lesson five. Finding current employees' public commentary is the highest-signal step short of talking to someone, and it costs nothing but search time. Direct outreach is the most valuable and most limited resource — a vague message gets ignored, but a specific, informed question (built on everything gathered in the first three steps) gets answered.

prompt: Which of these is the strongest evidence that a consultancy would be a good agency route for someone early in the field, versus one to avoid?

options.text: Its website has a polished "our values" page mentioning inclusion
Junior reviewers there are paired with a senior reviewer on their first several audits, with named review criteria
It has the most client logos on its homepage
It offers the lowest day rate in its region

hints: A values page costs nothing to write. A structured pairing process costs the company real time and money to run — which is what makes it good evidence.
explanation: A paired, criteria-based onboarding process is expensive for a consultancy to run — it means a senior person's billable time going toward training instead of client work — so a company that actually does it is showing real commitment to producing accurate audits, not just claiming to value inclusion. Client logos and values pages are marketing and cost the company almost nothing to produce. The lowest day rate is actually a mild warning sign for someone early-career: it often means junior reviewers are underpaying themselves without a mentorship structure in a company competing on price, which is a fast route to unaccountable, unsupported work.

prompt: A candidate lists "IAAP CPACC" on their resume. What does that credential actually verify, most precisely?

options.text: That they can audit a real product to WCAG 2.2 AA competently
That they hold foundational, cross-disciplinary knowledge of disability, accessibility principles and law — not hands-on technical audit skill
That they've personally used at least three assistive technologies fluently
That an employer verified their audit work directly

hints: CPACC stands for Certified Professional in Accessibility Core Competencies — read that name literally.
"Core competencies" is closer to a broad literacy exam than a skills test.
explanation: CPACC is a knowledge exam covering disability, accessibility principles, standards and law at a foundational level — it's a credible signal that someone has studied the field broadly, and a genuinely useful entry point for career changers with no portfolio yet. It is not a test of hands-on audit skill, which is what the Web Accessibility Specialist (WAS) credential targets instead, and it involves no employer verification of real work at all. Treating CPACC as proof of audit competence is the single most common overclaim on a resume in this field, and an interviewer who knows the credential will probe past it immediately.

prompt: A job posting states: "IAAP CPACC or WAS certification required." True or false: this is a hard, non-negotiable gate you should not apply past without one.

config.statement: A posting listing a certification as "required" is always a hard gate.
config.rubric: States the verdict and gives a reason grounded in how job postings actually get written, not just optimism.

hints: Who writes the requirements section of a job posting, and how often is it treated as a strict checklist versus an aspirational wish list?
Compare this to the well-known pattern of postings listing "5+ years of experience with a 3-year-old technology."
explanation: False, in the overwhelming majority of cases. Postings are frequently written by someone assembling a wish list, not the hiring manager who will actually screen resumes, and "required" in a bullet list often means "strongly preferred." The genuine hard-gate exception is government contracting work that explicitly requires DHS Trusted Tester certification by name for a specific federal engagement — that one is usually real, because it's tied to a contractual deliverable, not just a preference. Outside that specific case, a strong portfolio and clear interview performance regularly outweigh a missing certification listed as "required."

prompt: You have one strong finding from a personal practice audit: a modal dialog that traps focus incorrectly. Turn it into a two-paragraph portfolio piece that demonstrates judgment, not just that you found a bug. What goes in each paragraph?
hints: The first paragraph should read like a finding — task, method, impact. The second should show your thinking, not just the fix.
A portfolio piece that only states "I found X and it was wrong" reads like a checklist item. What would show you understand *why* it matters?
explanation: A strong version: paragraph one states the finding the way a real audit would — what task the barrier blocks, which access method revealed it, and the severity reasoning, mirroring the task-first structure from the foundations phase. Paragraph two shows judgment rather than just the fix: why this particular defect is easy for a team to miss even with automated testing in place (focus-trap bugs are invisible to markup-only scanners), what the fix actually required understanding about focus management, and how you verified the fix rather than just proposing it. The second paragraph is what separates a portfolio piece from a bug report — it's evidence of the same judgment a real audit requires, not just that a defect was noticed.

prompt: You want to publish a short case-study post about an accessibility audit you did for a paying client last year. What's the ethically sound default?

options.text: Name the client and site directly — it's your own work, so you own the right to publish it
Get explicit consent from the client first, or anonymise the site and findings enough that it can't be identified
Publish it anonymously without asking, since anonymising makes consent unnecessary
Never publish real client work under any circumstances

hints: Whose reputation is actually on the line if the post reads as a public callout — yours, or the client's?
"I did the work" and "I own the right to publish details about someone else's product publicly" are two different claims.
explanation: Doing the work doesn't create a right to publish specifics about someone else's product without their agreement — client engagements are typically confidential by default even without an explicit NDA, and a published finding can read as a public callout regardless of your intent. The ethically sound default is either explicit consent (many clients are glad to be named as a case study, and asking costs little) or genuine anonymisation thorough enough that the site and organisation can't be identified from the details given. "Never publish" is overcautious — anonymised, consented or sufficiently abstracted case studies are a normal and valuable part of a portfolio, and this module exists to help you do that well rather than avoid it entirely.

prompt: Put these steps of making a first open-source accessibility contribution in a realistic order.

items: Find a project with an active accessibility label or component library with a labelled 'good first issue'
Read the project's contribution guide and any existing discussion on the specific issue before writing anything
Write a small, well-scoped fix or a clearly-written issue report if you're not ready to submit code yet
Respond to maintainer feedback, even if it means revising more than once

hints: The single most common way a first contribution goes badly is skipping the contribution guide and submitting something that ignores an existing convention.
A well-written issue report, with no code attached, is a completely legitimate and valuable first contribution — it doesn't have to start with a pull request.
explanation: Reading the contribution guide and existing discussion before writing anything is the step most newcomers skip, and it's the one that causes the most wasted effort — many open-source accessibility issues already have a maintainer's stated approach, and ignoring it produces a rejected pull request that helps no one. A well-scoped issue report is a legitimate, complete first contribution on its own; it doesn't require code to be valuable, which matters on a day when reading and writing clearly is realistic but debugging someone else's codebase isn't.

prompt: Sort each proof strategy by the situation it fits best.

categories: Has 2+ years hands-on but no formal credential
Applying to a government contracting role

items.text: IAAP CPACC as a foundational, low-cost signal while building a portfolio
A published, anonymised case study demonstrating real audit judgment
items.category: Has 2+ years hands-on but no formal credential

items.text: DHS Trusted Tester certification, named explicitly in the posting's requirements
items.category: Applying to a government contracting role

items.text: Open-source contributions with visible, dated commit history
items.category: Has 2+ years hands-on but no formal credential

hints: Match the proof to what it's actually strong evidence of, for the specific gap a person has.
explanation: The career changer's real gap is credibility with no track record yet — a foundational certification is cheap, fast evidence of serious intent while a portfolio builds. Someone with real hands-on time has the opposite gap: they have judgment but no formal proof of it, so a published case study or a visible contribution history closes that gap far better than a knowledge-exam credential would. The government contracting case is the genuine exception where a specific named certification is often a hard requirement, tied to a contract deliverable rather than a preference.

prompt: True or false: recertification requirements (continuing education credits, periodic re-exams) exist mainly to keep certificate holders' skills current.

config.statement: Recertification cycles exist mainly to keep holders' skills current.
config.rubric: States the verdict and names a concrete way the field changes fast enough to justify it.

hints: WCAG itself has moved through multiple versions in the last decade, each adding new success criteria.
A credential earned once and never revisited would be increasingly stale evidence of current skill.
explanation: True, and it's a defensible design rather than a revenue tactic dressed up as rigor — though it's fair to notice it's also that. WCAG has genuinely moved (2.0 to 2.1 to 2.2, with 3.0 in development), assistive technology updates change what a reviewer needs to know, and a certification earned five years ago with no renewal says less about current skill than one actively maintained. The honest caveat: renewal also costs money and time on an ongoing basis, which is a real factor in whether it's worth pursuing for a given career stage — usefulness and cost aren't in tension here, they're both true at once.

prompt: Which of these portfolio pieces demonstrates audit judgment most convincingly to a hiring manager who reviews many resumes?

options.text: A list of WCAG success criteria the candidate has memorised
A short before/after case study explaining why a specific fix was chosen over an obvious alternative
A certificate of completion from a self-paced online course
A statement that the candidate "cares deeply about accessibility"

hints: Judgment shows up in the reasoning behind a choice, not in a list of things memorised or a statement of values.
explanation: A before/after case study that explains a real trade-off — why one fix was chosen over a more obvious one, what the obvious alternative would have broken — is direct evidence of the same reasoning an audit actually requires. A memorised list, a course-completion certificate, and a values statement are all real but weak signals: they show effort or interest, not demonstrated judgment on an actual case, which is what portfolio work is for.

prompt: A friend suggests you publish a blog post titled "5 Accessibility Fails at [Real Local Business]" using screenshots from their public website, without asking them first. Explain, in under 100 words, what's wrong with this specific plan and what you'd do instead.
hints: Whose product is being publicly named, and did they agree to that?
What would this same content look like anonymised, and does it lose any teaching value that way?
explanation: The plan names and publicly criticises a real, identifiable small business without their knowledge or consent — regardless of accuracy, this reads as a public callout, not a case study, and risks real reputational harm to a business that never agreed to be featured. It teaches the same lesson just as well anonymised: describe the pattern and the fix without naming the business, or better, ask first — many small businesses are glad for free, specific, constructive feedback if it's offered as a courtesy rather than published as an exposé.

prompt: Match each open-source entry point to what it's a realistic first contribution for.

pairs.left: A component library's labelled 'good first issue' about a missing ARIA attribute
pairs.right: Someone ready to write a small, scoped code fix

pairs.left: An open discussion thread on the ARIA Authoring Practices Guide about an unclear pattern description
pairs.right: Someone confident in writing but not yet in submitting code

pairs.left: A project's documentation with an outdated accessibility testing guide
pairs.right: Someone on a lower-energy day who can still read and edit clearly

hints: Each entry point asks for a different mix of skills — code confidence, writing confidence, or just careful reading.
explanation: Open-source accessibility work has entry points at several different energy and skill levels, which is exactly why it's a realistic contribution strategy for someone with variable capacity — a documentation fix on a low-energy day is just as real a contribution as a code fix on a high-energy one, and both build a visible, dated history.

prompt: A candidate has no certification, no formal audit job history, but three well-documented open-source accessibility contributions with visible maintainer approval. How should this be weighed against a candidate with a CPACC certification and no visible work?

options.text: The certified candidate is automatically stronger — a credential always outweighs unverified project work
The contributions are stronger evidence of applied judgment, though the certification still shows foundational knowledge worth asking about
Neither candidate is worth interviewing without both a certification and a portfolio

hints: Which piece of evidence is closer to what the job actually requires day to day: demonstrated applied work, or a knowledge exam?
explanation: Demonstrated, verifiable applied work — maintainer-approved contributions with a visible history — is generally stronger evidence of the judgment a real audit role requires than a knowledge-exam credential alone, which this module has built toward across every lesson. That doesn't make the certification worthless; it's still fair to ask about foundational knowledge in an interview. Refusing to interview either candidate discards real, if incomplete, evidence for no defensible reason.

prompt: Put these steps toward publishing an ethical audit case study in order.

items: Decide whether the source material is your own practice work, consented client work, or something else entirely
If it involves anyone else's product, get explicit consent or anonymise thoroughly enough to prevent identification
Write the finding using the task-first structure, focused on teaching the method rather than criticising the target
Publish, and be ready to take it down or amend it if the subject later objects

hints: Consent or anonymisation has to be settled before writing, not decided after a draft already names things.
explanation: Settling consent or anonymisation before writing prevents the common failure mode of drafting something specific and identifiable and only then trying to soften it — softening after the fact rarely fully removes what's identifiable. Staying willing to amend after publishing, even once consent was given, is a small courtesy that costs little and matters if circumstances change on the other side.

prompt: A take-home audit task asks you to review a signup form and "list the accessibility issues you find." You have four hours. Which submission is most likely to be marked well?

options.text: A raw axe DevTools export, unedited, listing every automated finding
A short, prioritised list of real barriers with task impact, severity reasoning and one or two well-explained fixes
The longest possible list of every conceivable WCAG criterion that could theoretically apply
A single critical finding, described in exhaustive multi-page detail, with nothing else submitted

hints: What has every module in this track built toward as the marker of real audit judgment — length, or prioritisation with reasoning?
A raw scan export shows you can run a tool. It doesn't show whether you can tell which of its results actually matter.
explanation: Take-home markers are almost always screening for the same judgment the rest of this track has built: distinguishing barriers from violations, prioritising by task impact, and writing findings someone could act on — not for exhaustive coverage or tool output. A raw scan export demonstrates tool literacy at best and actively signals a lack of manual judgment. An exhaustively long list of theoretical criteria reads as padding, not thoroughness. One finding described at extreme length, with nothing else submitted, under-uses the time given and doesn't show breadth of judgment across a form with several genuinely different barrier types.

prompt: In a live technical interview, you're asked to audit a page while sharing your screen and narrating your thinking. You hit a barrier you don't immediately recognise. Write the sentence you'd actually say, out loud, in that moment.
hints: What does silence, or a long unexplained pause, communicate to an interviewer watching your process?
Naming uncertainty out loud, specifically, is itself a demonstration of judgment — it shows you know what you don't know.
explanation: A strong response names the uncertainty specifically and states a next step, rather than either guessing confidently or going silent: something like, "I'm not certain whether this counts as a 4.1.2 issue or something without a clean criterion — let me check how it actually behaves with the screen reader before I commit to a severity." This does real work in an interview: it shows the task-first, evidence-before-citation habit this whole track has built, rather than either bluffing a plausible-sounding answer or freezing. Interviewers running this kind of exercise are frequently watching the process more than the final answer, and a narrated, honest "I'd verify this" reads as exactly the kind of judgment a real audit requires under real uncertainty.

prompt: True or false: if a product manager pushes back on your severity rating in an interview scenario, the strongest response is to immediately lower the rating to keep the conversation friendly.

config.statement: The strongest response to pushback on a severity rating is to immediately concede it.
config.rubric: States the verdict and names what a strong response actually does instead of immediate concession.

hints: What is the interviewer actually testing when they push back on a rating — your friendliness, or your reasoning under pressure?
There's a difference between defending a rating rigidly and defending it with evidence while staying open to new information.
explanation: False. Immediately conceding under social pressure, with no new evidence offered, signals that the original rating wasn't grounded in anything defensible — exactly the opposite of what this exercise is testing. The stronger response restates the specific evidence behind the rating (what task it blocks, for whom, via what access method) and asks what new information the pushback is based on. If the pushback surfaces a real fact you didn't have — a workaround exists, the affected flow is being deprecated — updating the rating in light of that is good judgment, not weakness. Caving with no new evidence, purely to keep things comfortable, is the failure mode this question is testing for.

prompt: An interviewer asks, "I noticed you requested extra time for this exercise — can I ask what that's for?" What does a candidate owe in response?

options.text: A full explanation of their diagnosis so the interviewer understands the request
Nothing about their medical situation — a simple confirmation that the accommodation is in place is sufficient
An apology for needing an accommodation
Proof of disability, such as documentation, on the spot

hints: What does the interviewer actually need to know to proceed — the diagnosis, or that the accommodation is agreed and in effect?
Compare this to how a workplace accommodation request is typically handled once approved — repeated justification usually isn't required.
explanation: A candidate owes nothing about their medical situation in this exchange — the accommodation, once requested and granted, doesn't require ongoing justification, and a question probing for more is one a candidate can decline to answer without it counting against them. "I appreciate you accommodating that, thanks" fully closes the loop. This mirrors workplace accommodation norms, where an approved accommodation doesn't need to be re-justified to colleagues on request; an interview process asking for more than that is worth noting as a signal in its own right, which the final lesson in this module covers directly.

prompt: Sort each interview-process behaviour by what it most likely signals about the employer.

items.text: An accommodation request is granted quickly, without requiring justification
The interviewer can name a specific recent example of a finding that got fixed
Every accessibility question in the interview is answered with "that's more of a legal question"
The team has one designated accessibility champion with no stated budget or headcount behind the role
The interviewer says accessibility work is "a priority this year"

hints: A vague positive statement ("a priority this year") isn't evidence on its own — ask what makes it checkable, the way earlier lessons taught you to distinguish signals by resolution.
The strongest positive and negative signals both involve something specific and costly to fake, echoing the module one lesson on remote-culture signals.
explanation: The strongest signals, in either direction, are specific and hard to fake: quick, unquestioned accommodation approval and a named example of remediation both cost the company something real to produce. "A priority this year" is a statement that costs nothing to make and needs a follow-up question — asking for a specific example — before it can be read as positive or not. An unfunded, unstaffed champion role is a classic pattern of an organisation naming the problem without resourcing the fix.

prompt: A take-home task gives you 90 minutes to audit a five-page checkout flow — clearly more scope than 90 minutes allows for full coverage. What's the strongest move?

options.text: Rush through all five pages superficially to show full coverage
Audit the one or two highest-risk pages thoroughly and state explicitly what wasn't covered and why
Submit nothing, since the time given is unreasonable

hints: This is the same staged-audit, honest-scope-statement judgment the foundations phase built — the take-home is testing whether it transfers under time pressure.
explanation: Auditing fewer pages thoroughly and stating the scope explicitly demonstrates exactly the judgment a real, time-boxed engagement requires — real audits are scoped and staged constantly, and an honest scope statement is a feature, not an admission of failure. Rushing through everything superficially produces a report that *looks* like coverage and isn't, which is precisely the dishonest-shallow-pass failure mode called out earlier in this track. Submitting nothing forfeits the exercise entirely and answers none of the question being tested.

prompt: Put these steps of a live, narrated audit interview in a realistic order.

items: Clarify scope and time available before starting
Narrate what you're checking and why as you go, not just what you find
State uncertainty specifically when you hit something unfamiliar, rather than guessing silently
Summarise findings by priority at the end, even if time ran out before full coverage

hints: Scope clarification belongs first for the same reason it does in a real engagement — everything after it depends on knowing what's actually being asked.
explanation: Clarifying scope first prevents wasted effort auditing the wrong thing under time pressure. Narrating reasoning throughout is what the interviewer is actually there to observe — a silent audit followed by a written summary defeats the purpose of a live exercise. Naming uncertainty specifically, rather than either guessing or freezing, is the moment most candidates handle worst and most interviewers weight most heavily. Ending with a prioritised summary, even incomplete, mirrors the honest-scope-statement habit from the take-home task.

prompt: True or false: a candidate who says "I'm not sure, I'd need to test that" during a live audit interview is showing weakness.

config.statement: Saying "I'm not sure, I'd need to test that" during a live audit is a sign of weakness.
config.rubric: States the verdict and connects it to what real audit work actually requires.

hints: What does an audit report that confidently asserts something untested actually risk, in real client work?
Compare to the earlier module's point about a reviewer's honest scope statement building trust, not undermining it.
explanation: False. Real audit work regularly requires verifying rather than guessing, and a candidate who says so out loud is demonstrating the exact discipline that prevents a false or overconfident finding from reaching a client. The actual weakness would be guessing confidently and being wrong, or going silent rather than naming the uncertainty — both worse outcomes than a clearly stated, specific "I'd need to test that."

prompt: During an interview, you're asked directly what your diagnosis is, framed as "just curious, for context." What's the strongest response?

options.text: Answer fully — refusing might seem evasive
Decline to share the diagnosis, and redirect to anything relevant the employer actually needs, such as an accommodation already agreed
Answer, but only partially

hints: What does the employer actually need to know to do their job, versus what they're asking out of curiosity?
explanation: A diagnosis is medical information the employer has no legitimate need for in most jurisdictions and no need for at all in this context — "for context" isn't a business requirement. Declining clearly and redirecting to what's actually relevant (an accommodation already in place, or none needed) is not evasive; it's a normal, appropriate boundary, and this module's whole point about what disclosure owes nobody applies directly here.

prompt: You're in the final interview round and everything so far has been positive, but you haven't yet asked how the team handles disagreement about a finding's severity, or what happens to a report after it's delivered. Write the two questions you'd ask, and say what a bad answer to each would sound like.
hints: What would you want to know about this team's actual remediation follow-through before accepting an offer?
A bad answer to a process question is often vague rather than obviously wrong — what would vague sound like here?
explanation: Two strong questions: "Can you walk me through what happens after an audit report is delivered — who owns triaging the findings?" and "Has there been a case where engineering or product disagreed with a severity call — how did that get resolved?" A bad answer to the first is vague ownership — "it kind of depends" with no name or process attached, suggesting reports go into a void. A bad answer to the second is either "that's never really come up" (implausible on any real team, and suggests findings aren't taken seriously enough to generate disagreement) or a description of the reviewer's judgment simply being overridden without discussion.

prompt: Match each interview moment to the behaviour that best demonstrates real audit judgment.

pairs.left: Asked to prioritise five findings in two minutes
pairs.right: Rank by task impact first, citing the criterion second

pairs.left: Asked why a finding you flagged might not be a "real" WCAG failure
pairs.right: Explain the barrier's task impact directly, without needing a clean citation to defend it

pairs.left: Given more scope than the time allows
pairs.right: State explicitly what was and wasn't covered, rather than rushing everything shallowly

pairs.left: Asked a question you genuinely don't know the answer to
pairs.right: Say so specifically, and state how you'd find out

hints: Every one of these maps back to a specific judgment habit built earlier in this track — the interview is testing whether it transfers under pressure, not new knowledge.
explanation: None of these responses require knowing more facts than a well-trained reviewer already has — they require the same judgment habits from earlier in the track (task-first prioritisation, defending barriers without a clean citation, honest scope statements, naming uncertainty) applied live, under mild social pressure, which is exactly what a hiring interview is testing for.

prompt: Which question, asked by a candidate near the end of an interview, most reliably reveals whether an employer would be a decent one to work for on accessibility specifically?

options.text: "Is accessibility important to you?"
"Can you tell me about a recent accessibility finding and what happened to it after it was reported?"
"Do you have a diversity statement?"

hints: A question answerable with a costless "yes" reveals nothing. A question that requires a specific, checkable example is much harder to bluff.
explanation: Asking for a specific recent example forces a concrete, checkable answer — either the interviewer can describe a real finding and its outcome, which is strong positive evidence, or they can't, which is itself informative. "Is accessibility important to you" invites a costless yes from anyone. A diversity statement's existence says little about whether accessibility findings actually get resourced and fixed.

prompt: You're booking a three-week audit engagement. Which weekly plan actually accounts for a real energy budget rather than an idealised one?

options.text: Schedule every day at full planned capacity, and treat any bad day as something to make up later in the same week
Build one buffer day into each week from the start, and stage the audit so any single day's work stands on its own
Schedule light work every day so no day is ever demanding
Front-load all the hardest work into the first two days, then coast

hints: A plan with no slack in it isn't a plan for a bad week — it's a plan for a good one that happens to always come true.
Staging the audit into self-contained pieces (from the foundations phase) is what makes a buffer day actually usable instead of just a hopeful label.
explanation: A buffer day built in from the start, combined with staging the work into self-contained pieces, means a bad day costs a day, not the whole engagement — which is the entire point of staging in the first place. Scheduling every day at full capacity treats a bad day as a debt to repay rather than a normal, planned-for variable. Uniformly light work every day wastes good-day capacity and often just extends the timeline without actually protecting anything. Front-loading assumes energy is highest at the start, which isn't a safe assumption for a variable-capacity condition and creates its own kind of front-loaded risk.

prompt: You've now written the same finding — a missing accessible name on an icon-only button — in eleven different audits over two years. Describe one concrete practice that reduces the *energy* cost of writing this finding again, without reducing its quality for the specific client reading it.
hints: The words change least; the specific location, screenshot and severity context change every time. What if only the second part had to be written fresh?
A template isn't the same as copy-pasting a generic finding — the goal is to save the boilerplate, not the judgment.
explanation: A strong answer: maintain a personal library of finding templates for the barriers you see most often — the general explanation of why a missing accessible name matters, the standard remediation guidance, a reusable severity-reasoning skeleton — and fill in only the client-specific location, screenshot and task context fresh each time. This preserves exactly the part that requires real judgment (does this specific instance actually block a task, and how severely) while eliminating the part that doesn't (re-explaining, from scratch, a mechanism you've explained eleven times already). The distinction matters: a template that gets pasted in without checking whether it actually applies to this instance is a shortcut that damages quality; a template that only replaces the boilerplate explanation, with the specific judgment written fresh, protects both energy and accuracy.

prompt: True or false: as the only disabled person in a client meeting, you're obligated to answer for how all disabled people would experience a product, not just to give your own professional assessment.

config.statement: The only disabled person in the room is obligated to speak for all disabled people, not just give their own professional assessment.
config.rubric: States the verdict and names what the reviewer is actually there to provide instead.

hints: What did the reviewer-profile lab in the foundations phase already establish about the limits of any one person's authority?
"I can speak to my own experience and professional judgment, not to every disabled person's experience" is a complete, legitimate answer.
explanation: False, and this connects directly back to the reviewer-profile work from the foundations phase: no single reviewer, disabled or not, can speak for the full range of disability experience — that's exactly why a serious audit combines standards, technique, and, where the budget allows, testing with multiple real users rather than treating one person's presence in the room as a stand-in for that testing. A reviewer can and should offer their own professional assessment and relevant lived experience; being expected to answer for an entire, hugely varied population is an unreasonable ask that's fair to decline, plainly: "I can tell you what I'm seeing and my own experience — for a fuller picture across different disabilities, that's what user testing with a range of participants is for."

prompt: A former client emails: "Would you be up for a free 30-minute Q&A with our whole engineering team on accessibility basics? Great exposure for you!" What's the strongest response?

options.text: Agree immediately — any exposure is worth the free hour
Decline the free version, and offer a paid version of the same session instead, named as such
Ignore the email entirely
Agree, but only if they promise future paid work

hints: "Exposure" is doing a lot of work in this request — whose benefit does it actually serve, and how much does it cost you?
Declining doesn't have to mean declining the relationship — it can mean declining the specific unpaid framing.
explanation: Naming a paid alternative directly is the strongest move: it keeps the relationship open, treats the request as the real, valuable work it actually is (a 30-minute session with an entire engineering team is genuine consulting, not a favour), and avoids the trap of "exposure" substituting for payment, which rarely converts into paid work at the rate the request implies. Agreeing immediately normalises being asked for unpaid team-wide sessions going forward. Ignoring the email forfeits a real opportunity to redirect it. Conditioning free work on a vague future promise almost never materialises into an actual contract and sets a precedent that the free version is the default one.

prompt: Sort each signal by whether it suggests a prospective client will actually act on audit findings, or is getting an audit mainly to check a compliance box.

items.text: Engineering leadership is included in the kickoff call, not just legal or procurement
The RFP explicitly asks for "a report we can point to if asked" with no remediation timeline mentioned
A remediation budget and rough timeline are discussed before the audit even starts
The client has a documented history of quietly shelving a previous vendor's audit report
The client asks what a realistic prioritised remediation plan would look like as part of the deliverable

hints: Look for whether engineering, budget and timeline are part of the conversation before the audit starts, or only the report itself is.
explanation: The pattern across the "likely to act" column is that remediation is planned for as part of the engagement, not treated as a separate, optional problem for later — engineering in the room, a budget discussed up front, and a request for a prioritised plan (not just a findings list) are all costly, specific signals a checkbox-only client generally won't produce, because they were never planning to act on the report in the first place.

prompt: An engagement is scoped at five days. You lose two to a flare. Which redesign best preserves both the client relationship and your own sustainability?

options.text: Work double time on the remaining three days to hit the original deadline anyway
Message the client with the gap, costed options, and a recommendation — the pattern from the foundations phase's renegotiation lesson
Quietly deliver a shorter, shallower audit at the original scope and price without saying anything

hints: This is deliberately the same renegotiation pattern taught earlier in the track, applied here to a whole-practice sustainability decision rather than a single audit.
explanation: Naming the gap, offering costed options and a recommendation protects the relationship (the client gets a real decision to make) and the reviewer (no attempt to silently absorb an impossible workload). Working double time to hit the original deadline is exactly the pattern this whole module exists to prevent — it treats the flare as a debt to repay rather than a normal planning variable. Quietly delivering less without saying so damages trust the moment the gap is noticed, and it usually is.

prompt: Put these steps of building a personal finding-template library in a sensible order.

items: Track which findings you write most often across engagements
Write a reusable explanation and remediation-guidance skeleton for the most frequent ones
Use the template for the boilerplate, and write the client-specific judgment fresh each time
Retire or revise a template if a client's specific context regularly makes it not quite fit

hints: The library only saves energy if it's built from genuinely frequent findings — building templates for rare ones wastes the same energy it's meant to save.
explanation: Starting from what's actually frequent avoids spending energy templating rare findings that won't pay off the effort. Keeping the client-specific judgment fresh each time is the step that protects quality — this is a savings measure on boilerplate, not a shortcut on judgment. Revising a template that keeps not-quite-fitting is what prevents the library from quietly degrading into the exact copy-paste failure mode the whole practice was built to avoid.

prompt: True or false: feeling frustrated at finding the same preventable barrier for the eleventh time is a sign you're burning out and should leave the field.

config.statement: Recurring frustration at a common, preventable barrier is a sign you should leave the field.
config.rubric: States the verdict and distinguishes normal recurring frustration from a genuine burnout signal.

hints: Is frustration at something genuinely, repeatedly preventable an unreasonable reaction, or a rational one?
What would distinguish ordinary recurring frustration from an actual burnout warning sign worth acting on?
explanation: False, as a blanket rule — recurring frustration at a genuinely preventable, repeated barrier is a rational response to a real pattern, not evidence of unsuitability for the work. What is worth taking seriously as a signal: frustration that's stopped being occasional and become constant, dread before every new engagement, or a template response that's calcified into not actually checking whether it fits. Those are closer to real burnout signals. Occasional frustration at the eleventh missing-alt-text finding is closer to normal — and, as this lesson notes, sometimes a signal that systemic advocacy work alongside audit work is worth pursuing, not that the work itself is wrong for you.

prompt: A conference organiser asks you to speak on a panel, unpaid, but covers travel. Under what condition does this fit as a reasonable exception to a default no-unpaid-work boundary?

options.text: Never — all speaking engagements must be paid
When it's a deliberate, occasional choice made for its own value (visibility in a community you value, genuine reach) rather than the default response to every ask
Whenever the organiser says it's a good opportunity

hints: The lesson isn't "never work for free" — it's "don't let free work become the unexamined default."
explanation: A occasional, deliberately chosen exception — picked because the specific platform or community genuinely matters to you, not because saying no felt awkward — is different from unpaid work becoming a habitual default. The organiser's own framing of the opportunity isn't a reliable signal on its own; it's framed as valuable by definition from their side of the ask. "Never" is stricter than this lesson actually argues for — the point is intentionality, not an absolute rule.

prompt: A prospective client's RFP says the audit "will support our annual compliance statement" and doesn't mention engineering involvement, remediation budget, or a timeline anywhere. Write the two questions you'd ask before deciding whether to bid on this engagement.
hints: What would you need to hear to believe this client actually intends to fix what you find, versus file the report away?
A vague answer to a specific, direct question is itself useful information — what question would make vagueness maximally revealing?
explanation: Two strong questions: "Who on the engineering or product side will be involved in reviewing findings, and when?" and "Is there a remediation budget or timeline already planned, separate from the audit itself?" Both force a specific, checkable answer rather than a reassuring generality. A client with real intent to fix things can usually name a person and a rough timeline; a checkbox-only client typically can't, or answers with something like "we'll figure that out after we see the report" — which, per this lesson, is the exact signal worth weighing seriously before committing real energy to the engagement.

prompt: Match each sustainability practice to the specific cost it protects against.

pairs.left: Building a buffer day into every week of an engagement
pairs.right: A single bad day becoming a missed deadline
Re-explaining the same mechanism from scratch every time it recurs

pairs.left: Naming "I can speak to my own experience, not all disabled people's" explicitly
pairs.right: Being asked to carry representative weight no single person can bear

pairs.left: Screening for remediation budget before bidding on a client
pairs.right: Spending real energy on an engagement whose findings were never going to be acted on

hints: Each practice in this module targets a specific, named cost — matching them keeps the module's ideas from blurring into one generic "protect your energy" instruction.
explanation: None of these are the same kind of protection — a buffer day protects against schedule risk, a template library protects against repeated explanatory labour, a stated boundary protects against representational overreach, and remediation-budget screening protects against effort spent on work that was never going to matter. Treating them as interchangeable "self-care" advice misses what each one specifically defends against.

prompt: Which best describes the relationship between this module's sustainability practices and the quality of the audit work itself?

options.text: Sustainability practices trade off against quality — protecting your energy means doing a worse audit
Sustainability practices protect the specific parts of the work that require real judgment, by removing energy cost from the parts that don't
They're unrelated — sustainability is a personal-wellness topic separate from audit quality

hints: Look back at the template-library exercise specifically — what did it explicitly preserve, and what did it explicitly cut?
explanation: Every practice in this module — staging, templating boilerplate, declining unpaid extraction, screening for real remediation intent — is designed to protect the finite, real judgment a good audit requires by cutting the energy cost of the parts that don't require it. That's the opposite of a quality trade-off: an exhausted reviewer working past capacity produces worse judgment, not more of it, which is exactly why this module treats sustainability as a professional skill rather than a personal indulgence.

prompt: A client's contract specifies "WCAG 2.0 AA." A candidate reviewer treats this as functionally equivalent to auditing against 2.2 AA, since 2.2 is newer and better. What's wrong with that assumption?

options.text: Nothing — later versions always fully supersede earlier ones in every practical sense
2.1 and 2.2 added new success criteria on top of 2.0 rather than replacing it, so a 2.0-only contract genuinely covers less — and conflating them can misrepresent what was actually tested
WCAG 2.0 and 2.2 test completely different, unrelated things
2.0 is stricter than 2.2, so auditing to 2.2 would under-deliver

hints: WCAG versions since 2.0 have been additive, not replacements — each new version keeps all the old success criteria and adds more.
If a client's contract says 2.0 and the report quietly tests to 2.2, what does that misrepresent about what was and wasn't actually verified?
explanation: WCAG 2.1 and 2.2 are additive: they keep every 2.0 success criterion and add new ones covering mobile, low vision, cognitive and other areas 2.0 didn't address. A 2.0-only engagement genuinely covers less ground than a 2.2 engagement — reasonable in a legacy contract, but worth naming precisely rather than assuming it's close enough to treat as equivalent. Silently testing to a newer version than contracted can misrepresent scope in either direction — over-delivering without saying so isn't neutral, because the client may be relying on the stated scope for their own compliance claims elsewhere.

prompt: True or false: once a finding is verified with one screen reader and browser combination, it's safe to assume the same result holds across all screen reader and browser pairings.

config.statement: A finding verified with one screen reader/browser pairing safely generalises to all pairings.
config.rubric: States the verdict and gives a concrete reason screen reader and browser behaviour can diverge.

hints: NVDA+Firefox and JAWS+Chrome are the two most common pairings in practice, and they don't always announce identically for the same markup.
An AT or browser update between when a finding was verified and when it's reported can also change the result.
explanation: False. Screen reader and browser combinations genuinely differ in how they interpret and announce the same markup — a pattern that announces correctly in NVDA with Firefox can announce incorrectly in JAWS with Chrome, and vice versa, because each pairing implements the accessibility tree and ARIA mapping slightly differently. A responsible report either verifies across the common pairings relevant to the client's actual user base, or states plainly which pairing was used and that others weren't verified — exactly the honest-scope habit built earlier in this track, applied to tooling rather than time.

prompt: A native HTML `<dialog>` element ships with new default focus and keyboard behaviour in a browser update. What's the correct response for a reviewer who has an existing finding referencing an older custom-built modal pattern?

options.text: Ignore it — the finding was correct when it was written, so it stays correct indefinitely
Recognise that a native element's changed default behaviour can affect whether an old finding, or its recommended fix, is still current
Assume all custom modal patterns are now automatically wrong and should be flagged

hints: A finding's correctness is tied to the environment it was verified in — when the environment changes, the finding may need to be re-verified, not assumed stable forever.
explanation: Platform-level changes — a native element gaining new default behaviour, a browser changing how it exposes something to the accessibility tree — can genuinely change whether a previously-written finding or its recommended fix is still accurate, which is exactly why a currency routine (covered later in this module) includes retesting known patterns, not just reading about changes. The old finding isn't automatically wrong forever, and custom modals aren't automatically wrong either — the correct response is to check, specifically, rather than assume in either direction.

prompt: Match each community or resource to what it's best suited to keep a reviewer current on.

pairs.left: The W3C's ARIA Authoring Practices Guide issue tracker
pairs.right: Emerging consensus on correct patterns for complex widgets

pairs.left: WebAIM's mailing list and screen reader usage survey
pairs.right: Real-world assistive technology usage trends and practitioner discussion

pairs.left: A disability-led accessibility community (Slack, Discord or forum)
A major accessibility conference's published talks (axe-con, CSUN)
pairs.right: Deeper dives and case studies, useful in longer, less frequent sessions

hints: Match by what kind of currency each source actually provides — pattern guidance, usage data, lived perspective, or depth — not just "a11y resource" generically.
explanation: Different sources serve different, specific parts of staying current — treating them interchangeably means over-relying on one kind of update (say, technical pattern guidance) while missing another (real usage trends or lived-experience perspective) entirely. A sustainable routine, covered in the last lesson of this module, deliberately draws from more than one type.

prompt: Put these steps of a quarterly currency review in a sensible order.

items: Check for WCAG, ARIA and major browser/AT release notes since the last review
Pick a small, representative sample of past findings or common patterns to retest
Retest that sample against the current environment
Write up what changed and which specific past findings, if any, it revises

hints: Checking what changed has to come before deciding what to retest — otherwise the sample is picked blind, without knowing what's actually likely to have shifted.
explanation: Scanning for changes first tells you where to focus the limited retesting time — retesting everything every quarter isn't sustainable, but retesting a sample chosen because something relevant actually changed is. Writing up which findings the review revises, last, is what turns the routine into something usable rather than just personal study — it's the artefact this lesson's lab is built around.

prompt: A client asks why their contract from eighteen months ago specified "WCAG 2.0 AA" instead of the now-current 2.2. What's the accurate, professional answer?

options.text: "That was a mistake on our part — 2.0 is now obsolete and meaningless"
"2.0 was current when the contract was written; 2.1 and 2.2 have since added further criteria on top of it, and it's worth discussing whether to update the target"
"It doesn't matter which version — they all test the same things"

hints: The honest answer names both that the contract wasn't wrong when written and that the target has since moved.
explanation: This answer is accurate on both counts: 2.0 wasn't a mistake at the time, and the newer versions are additive rather than a full replacement — which makes updating the target a genuine, worthwhile conversation rather than a correction of an earlier error.

prompt: You verified a finding six months ago using NVDA with Firefox. You're about to report it to a new client. What would you check or state before including it as-is?
hints: Has anything changed since the original verification — an NVDA release, a Firefox update, a change on the page itself?
What would an honest scope statement about this specific finding say?
explanation: Before including it as-is, check whether the finding still holds in the current NVDA/Firefox versions (a quick retest, not a full new audit), and state explicitly which pairing was verified if the report doesn't test across multiple combinations. If retesting isn't feasible in the time available, the honest move is to note the verification date and pairing rather than presenting a six-month-old result as freshly current — the same honesty this whole track has built around scope and method applies just as much to time as to breadth.

prompt: True or false: WCAG 3.0, once finalised, will be a simple drop-in replacement that keeps the same pass/fail structure as 2.x.

config.statement: WCAG 3.0 will keep the same pass/fail structure as WCAG 2.x.
config.rubric: States the verdict and names that 3.0 is being developed with a genuinely different scoring approach, while noting it remains years from adoption.

hints: WCAG 3.0 (sometimes referred to by its working title, Silver) has been described as moving toward a different kind of scoring model than the binary pass/fail of 2.x.
It's also worth being honest about the timeline — it's been in development for years and isn't close to displacing 2.x in contracts yet.
explanation: False, and worth stating carefully: WCAG 3.0 is being developed with a substantially different structure than the binary criterion pass/fail model of 2.x, aiming for something closer to graded scoring across a wider set of outcomes. It's genuinely useful to know this is coming, and equally important to be honest that it remains years from being finalised or broadly adopted in real contracts — treating it as an imminent replacement would be inaccurate and unhelpful to a client planning today's work.

prompt: Which is the more sustainable way to stay current on assistive technology changes, given a fixed quarterly time budget?

options.text: Attempt to test every finding you've ever written against every AT/browser update
Track release notes for the handful of AT/browser pairings most relevant to your actual client base, and retest a small representative sample
Ignore AT updates entirely since testing them all isn't feasible

hints: A sustainable routine has to fit inside a fixed time budget — which of these three actually could, realistically, every quarter?
explanation: Testing everything against every update isn't sustainable on any real time budget, and ignoring updates entirely risks reporting stale, inaccurate findings. Tracking the pairings that actually matter for your work and sampling a representative subset is the version that fits inside a fixed quarterly budget while still catching genuine drift — the same staged, budget-aware judgment built across this whole phase.

prompt: Sort each change by whether it typically warrants retesting existing findings, or is more of a background-awareness item.

items.text: A major screen reader ships a new release with changed default announcement behaviour for a common ARIA pattern
A new WCAG success criterion is added in a minor version update
A conference publishes a set of talk recordings
A community forum has an active discussion thread about a niche pattern you don't currently work with

hints: Ask: does this change what a *specific, already-written finding* would say today, or is it useful context that doesn't require retesting anything yet?
explanation: The distinction is whether a change is likely to alter what you'd write in an actual, existing finding today — a changed default AT behaviour or a new success criterion both can — versus something that's genuinely useful to know but doesn't require action on anything already written. Both categories matter, but only the first belongs in the retesting stage of a quarterly review; the second is exactly what casual, low-energy community engagement is for.

prompt: What's the main value of lurking in a disability-led accessibility community without actively posting, on a lower-energy week?

options.text: It provides no real value compared to active participation
It still surfaces real-world usage patterns and lived-experience context at a cost that fits a lower-energy week
It's only useful once you're ready to post actively

hints: Compare this to the earlier module's point about a documentation fix counting as a real open-source contribution on a lower-energy day.
explanation: Reading, without posting, still exposes a reviewer to real usage patterns, emerging discussion and lived-experience context — at a much lower energy cost than active participation, which makes it a genuinely useful, sustainable habit for a lower-energy week rather than a lesser version of "real" engagement.

prompt: Put these into the order a quarterly review should follow, cheapest and most informative steps first.

items: Scan release notes and spec updates since the last review
Choose a small sample of past findings likely to be affected
Retest that sample directly
Document exactly which findings the review revises, and which are unaffected

hints: This is the same order as the module's core lesson five sequence — repetition here is deliberate, since it's the routine the lab depends on.
explanation: Scanning for changes first is cheap and tells you where to focus; picking a sample based on that scan avoids wasted retesting; retesting directly produces real evidence rather than assumption; and documenting the outcome — including which findings are explicitly unaffected — is what makes the review usable as a real artefact rather than private study.
